en: The General Meaning of the Lotus Sutra, one fascicle (this fascicle contains 8,888 words; this chapter contains 4,172 words).
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Pílíng.
Preface to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter One.

Regarding the explanation of this single volume of the sublime scripture consisting of twenty-eight chapters, there are many different traditions; for now, I shall temporarily follow the Tiantai school.
Each chapter will be explained using three gates: first, stating the general meaning of each chapter; second, explaining each chapter...
Title. Third, an explanation of the internal text of each chapter, providing a brief structural analysis.
First, regarding the general meaning of the initial chapter: To begin with, the vast ocean of nature intermingles movement and stillness while coalescing into the True.

The distant Mount Jue embraces both principle and phenomena to disseminate the teaching; as the ocean of the teaching is inexhaustible, it casts its reflection by responding to the myriad capacities of beings.
These capacities vary in a thousand ways, yet they gallop forth according to the five vehicles to divide the path. Thus, for the Elder who permitted the chariot—

He opened the three vehicles and universally bestowed the wondrous vehicle of the single reality. Seeking his children with compassionate grace, he gathered his hundred dependents and entrusted them all with the wealth and estate of a single household.
This present sutra is the profound gateway for opening up the provisional to reveal the real, and the sublime maxim of the perfect and true ocean of fruition.
It encompasses the structural principles of all scriptures, just as the vast ocean swallows the thousand tides, and it broadly governs the multitude of canonical texts.
The essential pivot is like the great void embracing all existence. The literary garden is fragrant, blossoming with the flowers of the three lives and six stages of realization;
the forest of meaning is lush and verdant, bearing the fruits of the three paths and four virtues. When unfolded, the gates of the One Vehicle’s meanings are clearly distinguished.
Its brilliance outshines the sun and moon. When rolled up, it concentrates the profound pivot of the One Ultimate; when unfurled, it soars above the Wondrous High Peak.
Thus, every fragment of Maitreya’s inquiry universally benefits the lands of dust, and every clear precept of the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni) rains equally upon the present and the future.
Consequently, by mounting this Dharma wheel, one need not arise from a single place to travel everywhere throughout the boundless Dharma-realm; yet, entering those Dharma-gates, one...

A single thought-moment, when shifted, suddenly manifests an ocean of infinite kalpas; it may be called a precious ship that returns the flow to its source, and a silver candle that exhausts delusion and leads toward awakening.
The great purport of the teaching lies precisely here.
Second, regarding the explanation of the title: This present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the profound and secret treasury of the fundamental ground;
it is the wondrous Dharma of the provisional and the real of one’s own practice. Through the four lotuses and six earth-tremors, the gate of expedient means is opened;

through the three transformations and thousand surges, the stage of reality is manifested. Thus, all beings are universally enabled to see and hear it; for this reason, "Wondrous Dharma" (*Miaofa*) is first set forth as the title.
Next, it is likened to a lotus flower. It dispels the attachment to the provisional teaching of the "City of Manifestation" and eliminates the stagnant emotions of the "Thatched Hut.

It brings together all minor practices of various virtues and leads them back to the single vehicle of the vast and great. Those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties are all granted prophetic assurances (*vyākaraṇa*).

It reveals the profound treasury of secrets and is thus termed "Wondrous" (*miao*); it demonstrates the correct path of the provisional and the real, and is therefore called the "Dharma" (*fa*). It points toward the [Buddha's] long-distant...
The fundamental fruit is likened to the lotus; the perfect path of non-duality is compared to the flower. Sound serves as a Buddha-work and is termed a "sūtra.
At the beginning of this perfect exposition, it is designated as the "preface" (nidāna). As the meanings of the preface follow one another, they are termed "chapters" (parivarta).
The foremost among the assembly is called "the first. If one were to retain the Sanskrit sounds, it could be said:
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra*. Now, following the Chinese language, it is titled: "The Sutra of the Lotus Flower of the Wonderful Dharma," Chapter One: The Introduction.

Third, regarding the analysis and interpretation of the text: Now, the universal capacity of all beings reverently receives the intent of the Tathāgata, and the sublime thunder of the Dharma rains down the rain of equality.
This present sutra is that which was spoken by the True Buddha of long ago; it is the ultimate scripture of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
It was provisionally manifested through Ānanda and transmitted, its embryonic essence discerned and translated by Kumārajīva. Listen with clarity from of old.
This was requested by the Ear [of Avalokiteśvara]. It is mounted upon the protection of the White Samantabhadra.

It clearly reveals that the sentient beings of this world, responding to their capacities through the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), have summoned and moved the spiritual sages. This single body of scripture consists of eight fascicles and twenty-eight chapters.

It is divided into three major sections: the first chapter serves as the introduction; next is the "Expedient Means" (Fangbian-pin) chapter, ending with nineteen lines of verse from the "Distinguishing Merit" (Fenbie Gongde-pin) chapter. Altogether...

Fifteen chapters and a half are designated as the "Correct" (the *shōmon*). Three chapters from after the verses until the end of the sutra—totaling eleven chapters and a half—are for the "Circulation" (*ryūtsūmon*).

Furthermore, when divided according to time, there are two parts: from the initial "Introductory Chapter" (*Jōhon*) up to the "Peaceful Practices" (*Anrakugyō*), fourteen chapters constitute the "Trace Gate" (*sekimon*) which reveals the Real by opening the Provisional;
from the "Chapter on the Earth-Spurring" (*Jiyūjutsu-hon*) to the end of the sutra, fourteen chapters constitute the "Original Gate" (*honmon*) which opens [the Real].

The near reveals the distant; there are three sections for each of these two gates. First, regarding the three sections of the Gate of Traces (*jìmén*): the "Introductory Chapter" (*Xùpǐn*) serves as the introduction to the Gate of Traces.

Next, from the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Fāngbiàn pǐn*) up to the "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies upon Those Who Have Learned and Those Yet to Learn" (*Shòu xué wú xué rén jì pǐn*), constitutes the formal exposition (*zhèngshuō*) of the Gate of Traces.

From the end of the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" (*Fǎshī pǐn*) through the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (*Ānlè xíng pǐn*), constitutes the dissemination (*liútōng*) of the Gate of Traces. Next, regarding the three sections of the Gate of the Origin (*běnmén*): starting from the "Chapter on the Emergence [of the Stupa]" (*Yǒngchū pǐn*) up to Maitreya...
The first half of this chapter, which answers what was previously asked of the Buddha, serves as the introduction to the Root Chapter (*mūlaparivarta*).

Next, from where the Buddha addresses Ajita onwards, up until the prose and verse sections at the beginning of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit" (*Punyaparyāyaparivarta*), constitutes the main body (*samyak*). From the three verses following that until the end of the sutra is called the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*).

Now, regarding the three chapters of the Trace Gate (*jìmén*): the initial introduction (*xù*) has both a general and a specific aspect. The initial introduction consists of six parts: first, the essence of the Dharma heard, which is "Thus" (*evam*);
second, the person who upholds it, which is "I have heard" (*śrutam mayā*); third, the time of hearing and upholding, which is "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*);
fourth, the source from whom it was heard and upheld, which is "the Buddha" (*bhagavān*); fifth, the place where it was heard and upheld, which is Rājagṛha; [and sixth, the assembly of listeners].
"Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain" refers to this. "Six companions who uphold what they have heard" refers to those who departed together with the great assembly of bhikṣus. This section has two parts:
first, from "together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus" down to "King Ajātaśatru, together with several hundreds of thousands of followers," which clearly enumerates the assembly;
second, the eight characters "each bowed at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side."
This is the summary. Within the enumeration of the assembly, there are three parts.
From "together with great bhikṣus" down to "the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā also with [her followers]," the first clarifies the assembly of śrāvakas.
From "eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas" down to "bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, eighty thousand in all," the second clarifies the assembly of bodhisattvas. At that time...
From "Śakra Devānām Indra descended" down to "King Ajātaśatru and others," the third section clarifies the miscellaneous assembly.

Second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly" down to the end of the chapter, [it concerns] those seeking the three vehicles; this is the separate introduction.

Regarding the five intermediate introductions, from "At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly" down to "respectfully praised," the first clarifies the gathering of the assembly.

Preface. From "Then, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, he preached the Mahāyāna sūtras" down to "the emergence of the stupa made of the seven treasures," the second section clarifies the sequence of the manifestation of auspicious omens (*nidāna*).
From "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva... down to "the marks of supernormal power; whom should we now question?
the third section clarifies the sequence of the inquiry (*paripṛcchā*). From "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva... down to the end of the verses, [it asks] "what has been taught? the fourth...
The Preface to the Fourfold Exposition of Questions consists of two parts: first, the prose section (as detailed below);
second, from the passage beginning "At this time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning," follows the verse section, which comprises sixty-two lines divided into two parts.

The first part consists of fifty-four lines that versify the preceding questions (as detailed below), starting from the passage "When the Buddha emitted a single ray of light, I and the entire assembly... and so forth.

There are eight sections. [The first] is the verse requesting an answer (and so forth). From the passage beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke to Maitreya Bodhisattva" onwards is the fifth section, the introduction to the answers to the questions.
This contains two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. Within the first part, the prose, there are four sections.
From the passage beginning with "Maitreya" down to the end of the exposition of the great Dharma-meaning, the first explains the response given through reflection. From... [text continues].

"Good sons, from 'I, at the end of the [previous] kalpa' below, down to 'I have now manifested this auspicious sign,' the second section clarifies the brief answer concerning what was previously seen.
From 'Good sons, as in the past' below, down to 'Bodhisattva Seeking Fame, you are that very person,' the third section clarifies the detailed answer concerning what was previously seen.
From 'Now seeing this auspicious sign is no different from before' below, down to 'The Dharma for teaching Bodhisattvas, the Buddha...'"
That which is protected and remembered. Fourth, the clear and distinct definitive answer (and so forth).

From the verse spoken by Mañjuśrī at that time, the second section of verses consists of forty-five lines, divided into two parts. The first part comprises forty-one lines, which versify the detailed account of what was previously seen.
The answer from "I saw the Lamp-Light" downward consists of four lines, which versify the clear and distinct definitive answer (and so forth).
The Second Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "Expedient Means" (4,716 words).

I shall now explain this chapter by means of three sections: first, a statement of its general purport; second, an explanation of the chapter title; and third, an entry into the text for analysis and interpretation.
The first general purport is as follows: Now, the towering wisdom of the Buddha, when examined through its primary tenet, is found to be profoundly deep and immeasurable;
the vast gateway of his insight, when considered within the context of the three vehicles, is declared to be difficult to understand and difficult to enter. Thus, there are five oceans of profundity.
The qilin exhausts its strength at the base of the Eight Great High Peaks; the phoenix finds it difficult to soar to their summits.

Therefore, without waiting for the spring thunder, he vibrates the resonance of the fourfold Dharma for those hibernating in the three vehicles. Spontaneously proclaiming himself as the autumnal dragon, he pours down the sweet rain of the seven stages upon the fish of the seven provisional means.
Like the celestial net of Indra, the ten realms are encompassed in ever-deepening layers; like crystal, the One Vehicle is transparently clear.
Pervading ten lands, it remains hidden for a long time before being secretly chanted. A perfect pearl is tied within the robes of five thousand; it must be proclaimed openly.
A precious chariot is drawn by one great white ox, yet those of shallow wisdom—twelve hundred and fifty—give rise to doubts and become lost as to their destination.

The One Son of Deep Wisdom proclaimed what was yet uncompleted and questioned its progress; the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni) thrice halted him, purging five thousand [monks], while Śāriputra made three requests for the Ten Faiths of Diligence.
Thus, those who were but branches and leaves, or dregs and husks, forgot the pearl fastened to their robes and withdrew from the Dharma-seat.
The True Universal Vehicle (Ekayāna) abides in the assembly, holding the wealth of faith within its breast.
Thereupon, the majestic Dharma King exhorts one to believe, likening himself to the *tamdala* flower; his brilliant wisdom and practice act as a lotus to inspire joy.

Thus, the single great golden sun shines resplendently upon the five castes, and the fourfold silver moon appears brilliantly before the seven classes of beings. How could it be said that this excludes those of the parched seed?

Those who were silent encounter the rain of Dharma and sprout anew the seeds of Buddhahood; even those icchantikas at the end of their lives take the wondrous medicine and are restored to life in a future birth.

The teachings and scriptures serve as warp and woof, weaving the brocade of practice upon the loom of the five Buddhas; with the needle of wisdom and the thread of conduct, they stitch and adorn the embroidery of fruition upon the canopy of the three periods of time.
The original intent of all Buddhas is fully realized within this section; the great purpose of appearing in the world is entirely fulfilled herein.
This chapter shatters attachments and resolves doubts; the Lotus Sūtra is supreme among all. It opens the way for the deluded and illuminates awakening—who would dare contend with this scripture?

Its phrasing is concise yet its meaning is abundant; its principles are profound yet its practice is universal. It may truly be called the inconceivable, wondrous Dharma, a gateway to the teachings that is difficult to fathom.
Is it not precisely thus that the general purport of this chapter is intended?
Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "Fang" (方) means secret; "bian" (便) means wondrous.
To wondrously penetrate the secret is the true secret—the priceless treasure within one's inner garment, which is no different from the single jewel atop the King’s head.
Pointing to the hired laborer, it is said he is the son of the elder; likewise, there is no difference between them. Such words as these are secret and... [are wondrous].
"Exquisite. As the sutra states: "Only I know this mark; the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so. Cease, cease! There is no need to speak, for my Dharma is exquisite and inconceivable.

Therefore, using "secret" (*guhya*) explains the method, while using "exquisite" (*praṇīta*) explains the facility; this is precisely the intent of the present chapter. Hence, it is called the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*).

Third, regarding the analysis and interpretation of the textual content: from this chapter downward, ending with the nineteen verses spoken by Maitreya at the conclusion of the *Vibhāga-guṇa-parivarta*, and extending through the fifteen and a half chapters beginning with "The Buddha’s Name Resounds Throughout the Ten Directions and Greatly Benefits Sentient Beings," constitutes the second major section:

the Section of the Actual Exposition (*samyag-deśanā-bhāga*). If divided into two sub-sections of the actual exposition, this begins from the current chapter and concludes with the "Bestowal of Instruction" (*śikṣā-samādāpana*).

The "Prediction for Those Beyond Training" consists of eight sections; this is the section on the formal exposition of the Trace Gate (*jimen*). For now, we shall proceed with the immediate context of the formal exposition of the Trace Gate, which is divided into two major parts.

From the beginning of this chapter down to the passage "May you, for the sake of this assembly, deign to provide a detailed analysis," etc., is the first major section, clarifying the brief opening that reveals the One by means of the Three. This begins from: "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra."

"Since you have already made this earnest request three times, how could I not speak? and so forth. This concludes the seven and a half chapters of the sūtra-text from the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training.
The second major section clarifies the broad opening of the three and the revelation of the one.

Within the brief section on the opening of the three and the revelation of the one, there are two parts. From the beginning of this chapter down to the end of the verses, the Buddha, through the power of skillful means, demonstrates the three.
Vehicle. First, it clarifies the brief opening that reveals the One by means of the Three. This consists of both prose and verse sections. Within the prose section, there are two parts:

from the beginning of the chapter down to "the underlying intent of what has been taught according to suitability is difficult to understand," the first part clarifies the two wisdoms of the Buddhas—the provisional and the real;
from "Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood... onwards, the second part clarifies the provisional [wisdom] of Śākyamuni.
This consists of two actual wisdoms. The second verse praises the two wisdoms of the two Buddhas mentioned above (etc.).

From the passage "At that time, among the great assembly, there were various śrāvakas whose outflows were exhausted" down to "these, upon hearing this Dharma, gave rise to great joy," the second [section] clarifies how doubt gives rise to attachment and movement;
it raises doubts and requests [instruction] three times (etc.). The second [section], based on the extensive opening, reveals the Three as manifesting the One.

Section. Divided into three major parts: First, for those of superior faculties. This comprises the "Dharma-exposition" section, beginning from "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra" and continuing until the end of the second fascicle, concluding with the verses of the various devaputras:

"Whatever meritorious karma I possess, whether of this world or of past worlds, and all the merit from having seen the Buddha, I dedicate it entirely toward the Buddha-way. Second, for those of middling [faculties].

Regarding those of inferior capacity: there is the "Exhaustive Exposition through Parables. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret," and so on, until the end of the "Bestowal of Prophecy" chapter.
This constitutes three chapters of sutra text. Thirdly, for those of inferior capacity, there is the "Exhaustive Exposition through Causes and Conditions."

At the beginning of the "Parable of the City of Illusion" chapter, [the Buddha] addressed the bhikṣus regarding the distant past. This concludes the "Chapter on the Prediction for Learners and Those Beyond Learning.

Then, from the words "The World-Honored One, Lamp of Wisdom, I have heard the sound of the prediction," until "my heart was filled with joy as if drenched by nectar," there are three chapters of sutra text.
Regarding the first section, the Exposition of the Dharma, it is divided into five major parts: namely, the Exposition of the Dharma, the Acceptance, and so forth.

[This section consists of] the explanation (*vyākhyāna*), the exposition (*nirdeśa*), the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), and the joy (*prāmodya*). Regarding the first part concerning the Dharma, there are both prose and verse.
Within the first prose section, there are three parts. From "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: 'You have already... down to "...you should now listen well;
I shall speak for you," the first [part] clarifies the Tathāgata’s permission to preach. From Śāriputra’s words, "Yes indeed... [and so forth].
From "The World-Honored One" down to "I wish to hear it with joy," the second section clarifies receiving the mandate. From "The Buddha told Śāriputra:
'Such a wondrous Dharma as this'" down to "there is no other vehicle, there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle," the third section clarifies the Tathāgata’s extensive exposition.
There are five sections in total. First, the chapter on the four Buddhas, which extensively explains the two wisdoms—expedient and real—of the aforementioned Buddhas.

Second, the chapter on Śākyamuni, which extensively explains the two wisdoms—expedient and real—of the aforementioned Śākyamuni. This is divided into four parts according to the chapters on the four Buddhas.
From the passage "From such a wondrous Dharma... downwards, it is the same for all Buddhas of the ten directions.
First, the general section on the Buddhas consists of six sets of meanings and four types of explanations, including the fourfold equal explanation (etc.).
Second, from the passage "Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past, by means of countless skillful means and various causes and conditions... onwards, it clarifies the Buddhas of the past.
Section Heading. Regarding the middle [passage] (etc.). Third, from "Śāriputra, in the future, various Buddhas shall appear in the world" onwards, it clarifies the section heading on future Buddhas.

Regarding the middle [passage] (etc.). Fourth, from "Śāriputra, within the present immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-lands in the ten directions, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones... onwards, it clarifies the section heading on present Buddhas. Regarding...
[The middle section] (etc.). Second, from "Śāriputra, I am now likewise" onwards, it extensively explains the two wisdoms—expedient and real—of Śākyamuni Tathāgata as mentioned above.
This is explained through six meanings and four equalities within the middle section; it is not explained here (etc.).

Second, the verse commentary consists of one hundred and twenty-one lines and is divided into two major parts. The first part consists of four lines and one phrase, which is a verse [on the preceding prose].
The first part is the promised response. Next, there are one hundred and sixteen lines of three phrases, which provide the formal response to what was stated above.

This is divided into two sections. The first consists of seventy-three lines and one phrase, which comments upon the first section concerning the four Buddhas, beginning with "Now I am also like this.
The second consists of forty-three and a half lines, which comments upon the second section concerning Śākyamuni, categorized according to the four Buddhas.
The chapter consists of four sections. The first contains thirty-four lines and three phrases, versifying the first general section on all Buddhas, from "From countless kalpas past" onwards.
The second contains twenty-seven and a half lines, versifying the preceding section on the Buddhas of the past.
From "The various World-Honored Ones of the future descend" below, the third section consists of six lines and a half; this is the chapter on future Buddhas.
From "Honored by devas and humans" below, the fourth section consists of four lines and a half; this is the chapter on present Buddhas (and so forth).
From "Now I, too, am likewise" below, within the section on Śākyamuni, there are forty-three lines and a half, encompassing the entire marvelous work.
This serves as the basis for the seven similes that follow (and so forth).
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Three: The Parable (9,860 words; 6,591 words in the chapter). Now, this chapter will be explained by means of three sections:
first, an exposition of the general meaning of the chapter; second, an explanation of the title of the chapter.
Third, the analysis and interpretation of the text.
First, regarding the statement of the general meaning: Now, the Greatly Wise Śāriputra received the instruction from the Middle and Lower Vehicles to deliver his discourse;

the Greatly Compassionate World Hero, in response to the invitation of the [Buddha-]sons, expounded parables to illustrate this. Thus, the three vehicles were set up outside the gate, and the young children emerged.
"The burning house" describes the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles. "Providing a single carriage at the open space" refers to leading the sons to the site of enlightenment;
this clarifies the teaching of the One Vehicle. First one speaks of the burning house, and subsequently bestows the white ox-cart. This is the burning house of the triple world.

The abode of all living beings is the provisional chamber of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Sentient beings dwell within it; the pillar of their life-span serves as its foundation. Moistened by the four characteristics (*catvāri lakṣaṇāni*), it is worn down and decays;

the earth and water serve as its walls. Exposed to the two luminaries [sun and moon], it cracks and splits. The eight birds of pride (*māna*) spread their wings and soar over the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) upon the distant plains.
The eight insects of anger (*krodha*) fight with bared fangs amidst the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) in the vast wilderness. As for the dung-beetles of ignorance (*avidyā*), they...
They run about, deluded by the four inversions. Like foxes and wolves of craving, they embrace the five sensory objects and trample over them.
Like yakṣas of false views, they deny cause and effect like dogs that devour men. Like tīrthika-ghosts of attachment to precepts, they roam through the burning house as if engaged in play.
Like great ghosts of the view of a self, they calculate "mine" and lack shame or remorse. With the throat of attachment to views, they cling to their lives as a refuge. [The view of] extremes...

One sees the left horn of the ox-head demon clinging to the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, thereby extinguishing cause and effect; the right horn represents the view of extremes, grasping at past and future in a state of chaotic confusion.
The five dull beasts of ignorance startle the practitioner day and night, while the five sharp, wretched ghosts harass the wise man throughout the day and night.
Only the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, with his great kindness, can rescue one from these perils; and Avalokiteśvara, with his great compassion, protects.
To protect these [beings] from fear: all sentient beings of the three realms are the children of the Buddha; all conscious beings of the six paths are his heart.

Seeking with utmost sincerity, there is no other vehicle—whence could there be three vehicles? Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle—whence could there be five natures?

Those who slander the person and the Dharma shall suffer calamity in the three miserable realms; those who seek a friend and seek the Dharma shall find auspiciousness for ten thousand generations. This Chapter...
The general meaning is roughly as follows. Second, regarding the explanation of the title:
"Pari" (譬) means comparison; "yāya" (喻) means instruction through elucidation. By relying on this [the familiar] to compare that [the profound], one uses the shallow to instruct the deep.
Since this chapter specifically takes "pariyāya" (譬喻) as its name, it is called the "Parable Chapter" (Paryāya-parivarta).

Third, regarding the analysis and interpretation of the text: from the beginning of the chapter down to the end of the verses on “turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma” and so forth, this constitutes the second section, which clarifies the stage of realization within the cycle of the formal teaching. This section contains two parts:

first, the prose, which clarifies Śāriputra’s realization and his subsequent presentation [of it] (as detailed below); second, the verses, consisting of twenty-five lines, in which Śāriputra restates [his realization].
[From] "At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: 'I now [descend]... down to "The Dharma taught for instructing bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas.
This is the third section, clarifying the completion of the Dharma-exposition through the Tathāgata’s confirmation. [From] "Śāriputra, as for you in the future...
down to "That is none other than your own body; you should indeed rejoice. This is the fourth section, clarifying the completion of the Dharma-exposition.
The section on the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) consists of two parts. First, it clarifies the prose account of the Tathāgata’s bestowal of predictions.
Second, it clarifies the eleven and a half verses in which the Tathāgata reiterates [the predictions]. This begins from the passage: "At that time, the fourfold assembly... and so forth.

All merits derived from seeing the Buddha are dedicated toward the Buddha-way. Fifth, the section on the realization and understanding by the fourfold assembly during the middle of the Dharma-discourse (dharmaparyāya) cycle.
This contains three parts: first, the prose account of the realization and understanding by the fourfold assembly (*etc.*);
second, the six-and-a-half-line verse that reiterates the preceding (*etc.*). (The first of the three cycles, the Dharma-discourse cycle, is now concluded. At that time, from the house...
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret. This concludes the "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecy" (Vyākaraṇa-parivarta), the second major section.
It clarifies the completion of the parables for those of middling faculties; this section consists of four chapters. The first chapter is the "Parable of the Tathāgata."
This reveals the One by opening up the Three. The "Chapter on Resolute Belief and Understanding" clarifies the realization and understanding of the four great śrāvakas;

the "Chapter on the Simile of the Medicinal Herbs" clarifies the Tathāgata’s confirmation; and the "Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecy" clarifies the Tathāgata’s bestowal of prophecy. Regarding the first section, there are two parts.

Seven-jeweled goose-stupas fill the entire land. With the food of Dharma-joy, their hearts are satiated at will; with the draught of dhyāna-delight, their bodies are filled at the proper time.

The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Preacher (2,163 words). In order to explain this chapter, three sections will be employed:

and third, an analysis and interpretation of the text.
First, to state the general meaning: Lofty indeed is Śākyamuni, who spreads joy by vibrating the sound of his proclamation;

vast indeed is Bhaiṣajyarāja, who conceives delight upon hearing the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Thus, by the merit of a single phrase, one is granted the rank of the Unsurpassed; by the achievement of a single thought-moment, one is enfeoffed as the sovereign of boundless lands.
Like a pure practitioner scattering stars across the realms of dust, the Tathāgata’s special envoy—the Moon—illuminates billions [of worlds].
The sin of defaming the Buddha is lighter than a dispute over a blade of grass or a leaf; yet the karma of slandering others is weightier than contending over a massive boulder.

The wondrous flower of mirror-like wisdom laughs at the grove of offerings, while the precious fruit of omniscience matures within the forest of upholding the Dharma. The supreme dragon of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* has already shaken the valleys of the three vehicles;
now and hereafter, it shall speak as an elephant that tramples the peaks of the single vehicle. Its wind sweeps across the three turnings of the wheel, causing the banners of the six schools to fall.
The multitude surges forth with ten wonders, yet their tracks are disordered. The body of principle and wisdom entrusts itself to the scrolls of scripture to wander through the lands of dust.
The bodies of true and provisional response attain perfect enlightenment wherever the scriptures reside. Seeking water on high ground, one hears of the "ten suchnesses" and draws near to the mud.

From dry earth, sorrowful cries arise; awakening to the "seven parables," one beholds the water. Within the fragrant chamber of compassion, the five castes are sheltered together under the same roof. Patience...
Exquisite robes: seven people wear them together and occupy the same station. The vast couch of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnya*) allows one to sit at ease until death without obstruction.
The level bed of principle (*li*) permits one to accept [the teaching] with faith without abandoning indolence. The transformed fierce guardians ward off blades and staves from the practitioner.

The body of pure radiance manifests within the profound stillness. Though the words and phrases may be forgotten, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s instruction, the assembly in the empty and quiet place is heard by devas and nāgas.
The Dharma-preacher, protected by the Buddha, brings joy to the great multitude.

The disciples thus transformed follow their teacher’s training and behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The wondrous Dharma and perfect essence stand loftily and uniquely eminent, equal and impartial.
Mahāmati, such is the general purport of this chapter, which is firm and resolute.

The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa (2,632 words). In order to explain this chapter, three sections will be employed:
first, a statement of the general meaning of the chapter; second, an explanation of the title of the chapter;
and third, an entry into the text for analysis and interpretation.
First, to state the general meaning: This numinous tomb of the Seven Jewels rises from the earth to dwell amidst the Milky Way;

its five thousand chambers are adorned with railings and situated upon tiered steps. Furthermore, countless jeweled banners flutter like flowing rainbows, and ten billion jeweled bells chime with the clear resonance of the *gāthā*.
Golden and silver circular canopies hang in the midst of the sky, and lapis lazuli...
The caitya rose up to the four heavens. The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven rained down celestial flowers as an offering to the precious stūpa.
The eight classes of beings, including the nāgas and devas, performed music and offered praises to the stūpa. At that time, the towering temple emitted a deep, resonant sound.
In extolling Śākyamuni, he perfectly honors Prabhūtaratna; with profound eloquence, he realizes Great Wisdom.
Thus, the sixteen assemblies hear the sound of the stupa and are moved with longing; the eight classes of devas and humans give rise to doubt and feel a sense of urgency.
With solemn reverence for the Great Joy, the entire multitude awaits the resonance of the Dharma. The majestic Śākyamuni praises Prabhūtaratna and convenes the assembly.
Respectfully gazing upward, he delights in the discourse; desiring to behold the entire body of the majestic Great Awakened One, who gathers his emanations in assembly.
The Buddha of Prophecy speaks earnestly, emitting rays of light from between his brows to illuminate the ten directions. These vast emanations emerge from the assembly of attendants in the city;

for those devas and humans whose faculties are not yet mature, they shift them to other lands to purify their attachments to purity and impurity. For those sentient beings whose faculties are already mature, they reach out through the void to prevent their minds from becoming narrow.
The assembled Buddhas, having offered their consent, requested that the door of the stupa be opened. The Essential Body Śākyamuni responded to the request and opened the mani-gem door.
Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna shared half the seat with him; Śākyamuni, the Hero of the World, entered the body [of the stupa] to occupy the same chamber. Radiant were these two Honored Ones.
Lofty and towering, it stands high; a magnificent stupa, dense and elegantly poised, surpassing the fifteen great mountains in its majesty.
Its perfect wisdom of the One Vehicle excels the Three Vehicles even more than Mount Sumeru towers above the sea. The merit of merely upholding it is praised by all Buddhas;

the power of reading and reciting it causes one to dwell on the ground of pure goodness. It is the object of the "good eyes" of humans and devas, and is worthy of offerings from humans and devas—how truly marvelous!
The hesitation, the earnestness, and the utmost sincerity with which this was discussed are difficult to express in words; such, in brief, is the general purport of this chapter.
